subject: fvar and var types for arguments and returns

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: fvar and var types for arguments and returns
parts:
I want to work backwards from the functionals defined in
stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian, Hessian-vector
product, etc.) to the types that we need in arguments
for the auto-diff functions. In all of these applications, the top level
input to the function is a mixture of arithmetic types (double
and int) and a *single auto-diff type*. The single auto-diff type we'd call
them with would depend on the operation, but it will be one of:

var
fvar<double>
fvar<fvar<double>>
fvar<var>

Some of the functionals are written more genericaly, but
only in terms of these:

fvar<T>
fvar<fvar<T>>

All the same arguments will hold no matter what type T is.

If the inputs start out as homogenous auto-diff types (that is, just one
of the above fvar types) and doubles, then a simple inductive argument
shows that you only ever get a few patterns of auto-diff vars in
subsequent function calls.

For instance, suppose the auto-diff type is fvar<T>.
If the args start out as fvar<T> (and double), you only get
this:

(fvar<T>, fvar<T>) ===> (T,T)
(fvar<T>, double) ===> (T,double)

In particular, you won't ever call an operation between
a T and fvar<T>.

If T == fvar<T2>, then the same argument applies, and we
only get operations on the following types:

(fvar<T2>, fvar<T2>) ===> (T2,T2)
(fvar<T2>, double) ===> (T2,double)

As before, no mixing of T2 and fvar<T2>.

Therefore, I think these should be the signatures for operations on fvars:

fvar<T> op(fvar<T>, fvar<T>);
fvar<T> op(fvar<T>, double);
fvar<T> op(double, fvar<T>);
fvar<T> op(fvar<T>, int);
fvar<T> op(int, fvar<T>);

(Of course, those are all const references.)

We should not need to do promotion anywhere, so shouldn't
need signatures that look like this:

fvar<promote<T1,T2>::type> op(fvar<T1>, fvar<T2>);

We could use Boost's enable_if on an arithmetic type S
to combine int and double cases.

template <typename S, typename T>
enable_if<is_arithmetic<S>::value,
fvar<T> >::type
op(fvar<T>, S);

Does anyone see if I'm missing anything in this reasoning?

- Bob

As a side note, after going through the fvar files, I realized that some of them might not work with fvar<fvar<double>> and fvar<var> so Ill go through and write some tests for each function.

For fvar<fvar<double>> and fvar<var>, what do all the derivatives and values come out to? (i.e a.val_.val_, a.val_.d_, etc.)


Peter

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] fvar and var types for arguments and returns
parts:
If you think of an fvar<T> as (a, da/dx) for some x,
then an fvar<fvar<T>> is going to represent two first
order partials and a second-order partial:

( ( a, da/dx ), ( da/dy, d^2a/dxdy ) )

Initializations are

x -> ((x,1),(0,0))

y -> ((y,0),(1,0))

z -> ((z,0),(0,0))

The magic is that you only need the rules for first-order
auto-dif, and they just propagate.

I've attached some notes that explain the math in more detail.
This is going to go into a paper on our auto-diff system.

- Bob
